items.stem: Which of the following best describes "government failure"?
options: A situation where government intervention leads to a less efficient allocation of resources than the market outcome
A legal minimum price set by the government above the equilibrium price to raise producers' incomes
The loss of social surplus caused by the reduction in quantity below the free-market equilibrium, not offset by tax revenue
The area between the demand and supply curves over the units no longer traded (or over-produced) because of intervention
items.answer: A situation where government intervention leads to a less efficient allocation of resources than the market outcome
items.markingKey: A. "government failure" is a situation where government intervention leads to a less efficient allocation of resources than the market outcome.

items.stem: Distinguish between market-based policies and command-and-control policies.
items.answer: Market-based policies (taxes, subsidies, tradable permits) change incentives through prices; command-and-control policies (regulation, bans, standards) directly require or forbid behaviour.
items.markingKey: Market-based policies (taxes, subsidies, tradable permits) change incentives through prices; command-and-control policies (regulation, bans, standards) directly require or forbid behaviour. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Government intervention always improves market outcomes." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Intervention can cause government failure through poor information, unintended consequences, administrative costs or political motives.
items.markingKey: Intervention can cause government failure through poor information, unintended consequences, administrative costs or political motives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Identify the type of government intervention in each case: (i) a tax on plastic bags in Kenya; (ii) free primary schooling in Uganda; (iii) a ban on single-use plastic straws in the EU; (iv) a subsidy for public transport in Germany (the €49 Deutschlandticket).
items.answer: (i) indirect tax; (ii) direct provision; (iii) regulation; (iv) subsidy.
items.markingKey: (i) indirect tax; (ii) direct provision; (iii) regulation; (iv) subsidy.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how an indirect tax can be used to reduce the consumption of a good.
items.answer: Diagram: market for sugary drinks; specific tax shifts supply from S to S + tax (vertical distance = tax). Price paid by consumers rises from Pe to Pc, quantity falls from Qe to Qt; producers receive Pp = Pc − tax; government revenue = tax × Qt.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: market for sugary drinks; specific tax shifts supply from S to S + tax (vertical distance = tax). Price paid by consumers rises from Pe to Pc, quantity falls from Qe to Qt; producers receive Pp = Pc − tax; government revenue = tax × Qt. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

In 2022 several EU governments cut fuel taxes and capped energy bills to protect households from rising prices. Critics argued the measures cost billions of euros, helped high-income households most because they consume more energy, and weakened the incentive to save energy.
— Extract based on reporting of EU energy policies, 2022

Using the extract, explain two reasons for, and one possible consequence of, the government intervention.
items.answer: Reasons: protect households' real incomes (equity) and support firms; consequence: high fiscal cost / weaker price signal reducing incentives to save energy / poorly targeted support (government failure).
items.markingKey: Reasons: protect households' real incomes (equity) and support firms; consequence: high fiscal cost / weaker price signal reducing incentives to save energy / poorly targeted support (government failure). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "government intervention".
items.answer: Action by the government to change market outcomes, using taxes, subsidies, price controls, regulation, direct provision or nudges
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: action by the government to change market outcomes, using taxes, subsidies, price controls, regulation, direct provision or nudges. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why governments might intervene to change the consumption of particular goods.
items.answer: Some goods are over-consumed (demerit goods such as tobacco) or under-consumed (merit goods such as education) because of externalities or imperfect information; taxes, subsidies, regulation or information campaigns can move consumption towards the socially optimal level.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Some goods are over-consumed (demerit goods such as tobacco) or under-consumed (merit goods such as education) because of externalities or imperfect information; taxes, subsidies, regulation or information campaigns can move consumption towards the socially optimal level. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using Germany's €49 Deutschlandticket introduced in 2023 as an example, explain subsidies as a form of government intervention.
items.answer: A subsidised monthly ticket allowing unlimited regional and local public transport, funded jointly by federal and state governments. The subsidy lowers the price of public transport to encourage use, reducing congestion and emissions, at a cost to taxpayers.
items.markingKey: Context (A subsidised monthly ticket allowing unlimited regional and local public transport, funded jointly by federal and state governments.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The subsidy lowers the price of public transport to encourage use, reducing congestion and emissions, at a cost to taxpayers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to subsidies as a form of government intervention.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Governments intervene in markets mainly to raise revenue."
items.answer: Revenue is one motive, but correcting market failure, equity and supporting producers are equally important reasons.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: indirect taxes raise large sums (VAT, fuel duty). Arguments against: many interventions aim to correct market failure (carbon taxes, subsidies for vaccines); equity motives (minimum wages, price controls); supporting firms and strategic industries. Supported judgement: Revenue is one motive, but correcting market failure, equity and supporting producers are equally important reasons.

items.stem: What is a likely consequence of a price floor in agriculture?
items.answer: A surplus that the government may need to buy and store
items.markingKey: A surplus that the government may need to buy and store. Qs > Qd at the floor price.

items.stem: Explain the difference between allocative inefficiency from a price floor and allocative inefficiency from a price ceiling.
items.answer: A ceiling reduces quantity traded to Qs below the efficient level; a floor reduces quantity bought to Qd and, if the government buys the surplus, resources are used to produce output nobody wants – both create welfare loss.
items.markingKey: A ceiling reduces quantity traded to Qs below the efficient level; a floor reduces quantity bought to Qd and, if the government buys the surplus, resources are used to produce output nobody wants – both create welfare loss. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A price ceiling set above the equilibrium price causes a shortage." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A ceiling above equilibrium is not binding: the market simply clears at the equilibrium price below the ceiling.
items.markingKey: A ceiling above equilibrium is not binding: the market simply clears at the equilibrium price below the ceiling. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Data from a consumer survey and from producers in Mumbai give the demand function Qd = 90 − 2P and the supply function Qs = −30 + 3P for bottled water (P in $; Q in thousands per month). The government sets a minimum price of $25. Calculate the surplus.
Berlin froze rents for five years in 2020 (the Mietendeckel), before the law was overturned in 2021. Predict two consequences of such a policy.
items.answer: Shortage of rental flats (more demand, fewer flats offered for rent – some converted to owner-occupation); queues and long searches, fall in maintenance, black-market payments, less new construction.
items.markingKey: Shortage of rental flats (more demand, fewer flats offered for rent – some converted to owner-occupation); queues and long searches, fall in maintenance, black-market payments, less new construction.

items.stem: Using Venezuela's price controls on basic foods as an example, explain the consequences of price ceilings.
items.answer: Prices of flour, milk and other staples were fixed below market levels; by 2016 shelves were empty and long queues formed. Price below equilibrium cut quantity supplied and raised quantity demanded, creating shortages and black markets.
items.markingKey: Context (Prices of flour, milk and other staples were fixed below market levels; by 2016 shelves were empty and long queues formed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Price below equilibrium cut quantity supplied and raised quantity demanded, creating shortages and black markets. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the consequences of price ceilings.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

In 2022 Germany raised its national minimum wage from €9.82 to €12 an hour, an increase of about 22%. The government estimated that around 6 million workers would benefit. Some small businesses in hospitality said they would cut hours or raise prices.
— Extract based on reporting of Germany's minimum wage increase

Using a diagram, explain the possible effect of the higher minimum wage on the labour market.
items.answer: Labour market diagram: wage on vertical axis, quantity of labour on horizontal; the minimum wage set above equilibrium raises quantity supplied and reduces quantity demanded, creating a surplus of labour (unemployment); the size depends on elasticities; workers who keep jobs earn more.
items.markingKey: Labour market diagram: wage on vertical axis, quantity of labour on horizontal; the minimum wage set above equilibrium raises quantity supplied and reduces quantity demanded, creating a surplus of labour (unemployment); the size depends on elasticities; workers who keep jobs earn more. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that Minimum wages do more good than harm?
items.answer: Moderate minimum wages appear to raise incomes with little job loss, but very high minimum wages relative to median wages risk unemployment.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: raise incomes of low-paid workers and reduce in-work poverty; may increase productivity and reduce staff turnover; evidence (Card and Krueger; UK national living wage) suggests small employment effects. Arguments against: may cause unemployment for low-skilled and young workers; higher prices for consumers; may encourage informal employment in developing countries. Supported judgement: Moderate minimum wages appear to raise incomes with little job loss, but very high minimum wages relative to median wages risk unemployment. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Methods of allocating a good when price cannot do so, such as queues, waiting lists, lotteries or favouritism"?
items.answer: non-price rationing
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of non-price rationing.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a minimum wage might increase unemployment.
items.answer: Set above the equilibrium wage, it raises the quantity of labour supplied and reduces the quantity demanded by employers, creating a surplus of labour (unemployment), especially among low-skilled workers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Set above the equilibrium wage, it raises the quantity of labour supplied and reduces the quantity demanded by employers, creating a surplus of labour (unemployment), especially among low-skilled workers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a minimum wage for low-paid workers.
items.answer: Advantage: higher income for those who keep their jobs, reducing poverty and inequality; disadvantage: possible job losses or fewer hours as employers demand less labour.
items.markingKey: Advantage: higher income for those who keep their jobs, reducing poverty and inequality; disadvantage: possible job losses or fewer hours as employers demand less labour.

items.stem: With reference to the EU's Common Agricultural Policy in the 1980s, explain how it illustrates the consequences of price floors in agriculture.
items.answer: Guaranteed prices led to large surpluses known as 'butter mountains' and 'wine lakes' that the EU bought and stored. Prices above equilibrium encouraged over-production; the surplus cost taxpayers and was sometimes dumped on world markets.
items.markingKey: Context (Guaranteed prices led to large surpluses known as 'butter mountains' and 'wine lakes' that the EU bought and stored.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Prices above equilibrium encouraged over-production; the surplus cost taxpayers and was sometimes dumped on world markets. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the consequences of price floors in agriculture.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that rent controls are an effective way to make housing affordable.
items.answer: Rent controls help sitting tenants in the short run, but in the long run they reduce supply; increasing housing supply and targeted subsidies are usually more effective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lower rents for existing tenants; protects low-income households from rapid rent rises; greater security of tenure. Arguments against: shortages and long waiting lists; less investment in maintenance and new rental housing; black markets and discrimination between tenants; benefits not targeted at the poorest. Judgement: Rent controls help sitting tenants in the short run, but in the long run they reduce supply; increasing housing supply and targeted subsidies are usually more effective. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An indirect tax charged as a percentage of the price, such as VAT, which shifts the supply curve up by a widening amount as price rises"?
items.answer: ad valorem tax
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of ad valorem tax.

items.stem: Distinguish between a specific tax and an ad valorem tax.
items.answer: A specific tax is a fixed amount per unit, shifting supply up in parallel; an ad valorem tax is a percentage of price, so the vertical shift increases with price (curves diverge).
items.markingKey: A specific tax is a fixed amount per unit, shifting supply up in parallel; an ad valorem tax is a percentage of price, so the vertical shift increases with price (curves diverge). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the producer burden and the consumer burden of a tax.
items.answer: The consumer burden is the increase in price paid per unit times quantity sold; the producer burden is the fall in price received per unit times quantity.
items.markingKey: The consumer burden is the increase in price paid per unit times quantity sold; the producer burden is the fall in price received per unit times quantity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "When a specific tax of $2 is imposed, the price consumers pay always rises by $2." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The price paid rises by the full $2 only if demand is perfectly inelastic or supply perfectly elastic; normally the burden is shared and the price rises by less than $2.
items.markingKey: The price paid rises by the full $2 only if demand is perfectly inelastic or supply perfectly elastic; normally the burden is shared and the price rises by less than $2. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

In 2022 Indonesia spent over $30 billion on fuel subsidies, keeping petrol prices far below world levels. In September 2022 the government raised subsidised petrol prices by about 30%, arguing that most of the subsidy benefited wealthier households who own cars.
— Extract based on reporting of Indonesia's fuel subsidies

Using the extract, explain two disadvantages of the fuel subsidy.
items.answer: Large fiscal cost/opportunity cost of $30bn (could fund health, education); poorly targeted – benefits richer car owners (inequity); also over-consumption of fuel and emissions (negative externality).
items.markingKey: Large fiscal cost/opportunity cost of $30bn (could fund health, education); poorly targeted – benefits richer car owners (inequity); also over-consumption of fuel and emissions (negative externality). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: India subsidises fertiliser so that farmers pay well below the cost of production. Outline one benefit and one cost of this subsidy.
items.answer: Benefit: lower costs for farmers, higher crop output and food security; cost: large fiscal burden (opportunity cost), overuse of fertiliser damaging soil and water.
items.markingKey: Benefit: lower costs for farmers, higher crop output and food security; cost: large fiscal burden (opportunity cost), overuse of fertiliser damaging soil and water.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Subsidies to producers are a waste of taxpayers' money."
items.answer: Subsidies are justified where there are positive externalities or strategic needs, but should be targeted, time-limited and evaluated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: opportunity cost of government spending; firms may become inefficient and dependent; can cause overproduction and welfare loss. Arguments against: correct positive externalities (renewable energy, vaccines); support strategic industries and employment; lower prices for consumers of necessities. Supported judgement: Subsidies are justified where there are positive externalities or strategic needs, but should be targeted, time-limited and evaluated.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that subsidies to producers are a waste of taxpayers' money.
items.answer: Subsidies are justified where there are positive externalities or strategic needs, but should be targeted, time-limited and evaluated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: opportunity cost of government spending; firms may become inefficient and dependent; can cause overproduction and welfare loss. items.stem: Briefly explain why governments subsidise producers of goods such as solar panels.
items.answer: To lower costs and prices, increase production and consumption of goods with positive externalities, support strategic industries and jobs, and help meet climate targets.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: To lower costs and prices, increase production and consumption of goods with positive externalities, support strategic industries and jobs, and help meet climate targets. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the producer burden and the consumer burden of a tax.
items.answer: The consumer burden is the increase in price paid per unit times quantity sold; the producer burden is the fall in price received per unit times quantity.
items.markingKey: The consumer burden is the increase in price paid per unit times quantity sold; the producer burden is the fall in price received per unit times quantity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A researcher estimates that the weekly demand for bus tickets in Singapore is Qd = 124 − 4P and the weekly supply is Qs = −20 + 2P (P in $, Q in thousands). The government grants producers a subsidy of $3 per unit. Calculate the new price paid by consumers, the price received by producers, the new quantity and the total cost of the subsidy to the government.
A student claims that Subsidies only benefit producers because the money is paid to them. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The subsidy shifts supply down, lowering the price consumers pay, so consumers also gain; the split depends on elasticities.
items.markingKey: The subsidy shifts supply down, lowering the price consumers pay, so consumers also gain; the split depends on elasticities. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: If Pe = $20 and Qe = 100, and after a tax Pc = $23 and Q = 80, what is the change in consumer expenditure?
items.answer: It falls by $160
items.markingKey: It falls by $160. Before 2,000; after 23 × 80 = 1,840.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the government revenue from a tax is less than the tax per unit multiplied by the original quantity.
items.answer: The tax raises the price paid and reduces quantity bought; revenue is the tax per unit times the new, lower quantity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The tax raises the price paid and reduces quantity bought; revenue is the tax per unit times the new, lower quantity. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between consumer expenditure and producer revenue (with a tax).
items.answer: With a tax, consumer expenditure = price paid × quantity; producer revenue = price received × quantity. The difference is the tax revenue.
items.markingKey: With a tax, consumer expenditure = price paid × quantity; producer revenue = price received × quantity. The difference is the tax revenue. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Hypothetical data for a market for wheat: before intervention P = $200 per tonne and Q = 10 million tonnes. The government sets a minimum price of $240; quantity supplied rises to 11.5 million tonnes and quantity demanded falls to 9 million tonnes. The government buys the surplus.
— Hypothetical data

Calculate the cost to the government and the change in farmers' revenue.
items.answer: Surplus = 2.5m tonnes; cost = $240 × 2.5m = $600m. Farmers' revenue: before $2,000m; after $240 × 11.5m = $2,760m, a rise of $760m.
items.markingKey: Surplus = 2.5m tonnes; cost = $240 × 2.5m = $600m. Farmers' revenue: before $2,000m; after $240 × 11.5m = $2,760m, a rise of $760m. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Alessia writes: "The welfare loss of a tax equals the tax revenue." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Tax revenue is a transfer from consumers and producers to the government; the welfare loss is only the triangle of surplus lost on units no longer traded.
items.markingKey: Tax revenue is a transfer from consumers and producers to the government; the welfare loss is only the triangle of surplus lost on units no longer traded. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Calculating the effects of intervention on stakeholders is essential for good policy-making.
items.answer: Quantifying stakeholder effects improves policy decisions, but must be combined with judgement about unquantifiable and distributional effects.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows who gains and loses and by how much; allows comparison of alternative policies; reveals welfare loss and fiscal cost. Arguments against: calculations rely on estimated functions; some effects (health, environment) are hard to quantify; political and equity judgements are still needed. Supported judgement: Quantifying stakeholder effects improves policy decisions, but must be combined with judgement about unquantifiable and distributional effects.

items.stem: Define the term "government expenditure on a subsidy".
items.answer: The subsidy per unit multiplied by the quantity produced after the subsidy
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the subsidy per unit multiplied by the quantity produced after the subsidy. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims that the welfare loss of a tax equals the tax revenue. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Tax revenue is a transfer from consumers and producers to the government; the welfare loss is only the triangle of surplus lost on units no longer traded.
items.markingKey: Tax revenue is a transfer from consumers and producers to the government; the welfare loss is only the triangle of surplus lost on units no longer traded. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Before a tax, P = $15 and Q = 2,000. After a $4 tax, P = $18 and Q = 1,600. Calculate the consumer burden, the producer burden and government revenue.
items.answer: Consumer burden (18 − 15) × 1,600 = $4,800; producer price 14, producer burden (15 − 14) × 1,600 = $1,600; revenue 4 × 1,600 = $6,400.
items.markingKey: Consumer burden (18 − 15) × 1,600 = $4,800; producer price 14, producer burden (15 − 14) × 1,600 = $1,600; revenue 4 × 1,600 = $6,400.

items.stem: A government is choosing between a price ceiling and a subsidy to make a basic food more affordable. Using calculations from a hypothetical example, compare the effects on consumers, producers and the government.
items.answer: Ceiling: lower price but shortage, lower producer revenue, no direct cost but welfare loss and black market; subsidy: lower price with more output, producers gain, government cost = subsidy × Q. Calculation with linear functions and comparison; recommendation.
items.markingKey: Ceiling: lower price but shortage, lower producer revenue, no direct cost but welfare loss and black market; subsidy: lower price with more output, producers gain, government cost = subsidy × Q. Calculation with linear functions and comparison; recommendation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "minimum wage"?
options: The area between the demand and supply curves over the units no longer traded (or over-produced) because of intervention
An illegal market in which goods are sold at prices above the legal maximum
A situation where government intervention leads to a less efficient allocation of resources than the market outcome
A legal floor on the wage rate employers can pay workers
items.answer: A legal floor on the wage rate employers can pay workers
items.markingKey: D. "minimum wage" is a legal floor on the wage rate employers can pay workers.

items.stem: Which of the following is the government revenue from a specific tax?
options: Tax per unit × quantity sold after the tax
items.answer: Tax per unit × quantity sold after the tax
items.markingKey: D. Revenue is the rectangle between the consumer and producer prices up to the new quantity.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of direct provision?
options: A ban on lead in petrol
items.answer: A government-run public hospital
items.markingKey: A. The government itself supplies the service.

items.stem: Distinguish between government expenditure on a subsidy and government revenue from a tax.
items.answer: A tax raises revenue equal to tax × new quantity; a subsidy costs the government subsidy × new (higher) quantity.
items.markingKey: A tax raises revenue equal to tax × new quantity; a subsidy costs the government subsidy × new (higher) quantity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: The tax raises the price paid and lowers the price received, reducing quantity below the free-market level; units between the new and original quantity, which consumers valued above their cost, are no longer produced, so social surplus is lost beyond the revenue raised.

items.stem: Using the UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy (2018) as an example, explain the effects of a specific tax.
items.answer: A tax of 18p per litre on drinks with 5g+ sugar per 100ml and 24p for 8g+ led many firms to reformulate; the sugar sold in soft drinks fell by around 35-45%. The tax increased costs for high-sugar drinks; firms avoided it by cutting sugar, so consumption of sugar fell while revenue was lower than forecast.
items.markingKey: Context (A tax of 18p per litre on drinks with 5g+ sugar per 100ml and 24p for 8g+ led many firms to reformulate; the sugar sold in soft drinks fell by around 35-45%.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The tax increased costs for high-sugar drinks; firms avoided it by cutting sugar, so consumption of sugar fell while revenue was lower than forecast. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effects of a specific tax.

items.stem: Using Thailand's rice pledging scheme (2011-2014) as an example, explain the costs of price support for stakeholders.
items.answer: The government bought rice from farmers at prices around 50% above market levels, building up huge stocks and losses estimated at over $15 billion. Farmers gained higher revenue, but taxpayers bore the cost of buying and storing the surplus, and Thailand lost export market share.
items.markingKey: Context (The government bought rice from farmers at prices around 50% above market levels, building up huge stocks and losses estimated at over $15 billion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Farmers gained higher revenue, but taxpayers bore the cost of buying and storing the surplus, and Thailand lost export market share. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the costs of price support for stakeholders.

items.stem: A student claims that a price ceiling set above the equilibrium price causes a shortage. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A ceiling above equilibrium is not binding: the market simply clears at the equilibrium price below the ceiling.
items.markingKey: A ceiling above equilibrium is not binding: the market simply clears at the equilibrium price below the ceiling. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that when a specific tax of $2 is imposed, the price consumers pay always rises by $2. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The price paid rises by the full $2 only if demand is perfectly inelastic or supply perfectly elastic; normally the burden is shared and the price rises by less than $2.
items.markingKey: The price paid rises by the full $2 only if demand is perfectly inelastic or supply perfectly elastic; normally the burden is shared and the price rises by less than $2. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "Government intervention always improves market outcomes." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Intervention can cause government failure through poor information, unintended consequences, administrative costs or political motives.
items.markingKey: Intervention can cause government failure through poor information, unintended consequences, administrative costs or political motives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Thailand's rice pledging scheme (2011-2014) shows the costs of price support for stakeholders.
items.answer: The government bought rice from farmers at prices around 50% above market levels, building up huge stocks and losses estimated at over $15 billion. Farmers gained higher revenue, but taxpayers bore the cost of buying and storing the surplus, and Thailand lost export market share.
items.markingKey: Context (The government bought rice from farmers at prices around 50% above market levels, building up huge stocks and losses estimated at over $15 billion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Farmers gained higher revenue, but taxpayers bore the cost of buying and storing the surplus, and Thailand lost export market share. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the costs of price support for stakeholders.

items.stem: Using a diagram, explain the effects of a maximum price on rice on consumers, producers and the government.
items.answer: Ceiling below equilibrium: Qd rises, Qs falls, shortage; consumers who buy pay less (gain), those who cannot buy lose; producers receive lower price and revenue; government may need to ration, subsidise producers or provide rice directly; black markets; welfare loss.
items.markingKey: Ceiling below equilibrium: Qd rises, Qs falls, shortage; consumers who buy pay less (gain), those who cannot buy lose; producers receive lower price and revenue; government may need to ration, subsidise producers or provide rice directly; black markets; welfare loss.

items.stem: "Subsidies to producers are a waste of taxpayers' money." Discuss.
items.answer: Subsidies are justified where there are positive externalities or strategic needs, but should be targeted, time-limited and evaluated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: opportunity cost of government spending; firms may become inefficient and dependent; can cause overproduction and welfare loss. Arguments against: correct positive externalities (renewable energy, vaccines); support strategic industries and employment; lower prices for consumers of necessities. Supported judgement: Subsidies are justified where there are positive externalities or strategic needs, but should be targeted, time-limited and evaluated. items.stem: To what extent is it true that Market-based policies are more effective than regulation in changing behaviour?
items.answer: Market-based policies are often more efficient, but regulation is better when harm is severe or certainty is required; combinations are common.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: taxes and subsidies use the price mechanism and allow flexibility; raise revenue; encourage cost-effective changes (firms that can cut cheaply do most). Arguments against: regulation gives certainty (bans on dangerous products); effects of taxes depend on PED; monitoring and enforcement still needed. Supported judgement: Market-based policies are often more efficient, but regulation is better when harm is severe or certainty is required; combinations are common. items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that calculating the effects of intervention on stakeholders is essential for good policy-making.
items.answer: Quantifying stakeholder effects improves policy decisions, but must be combined with judgement about unquantifiable and distributional effects.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows who gains and loses and by how much; allows comparison of alternative policies; reveals welfare loss and fiscal cost. Arguments against: calculations rely on estimated functions; some effects (health, environment) are hard to quantify; political and equity judgements are still needed. Judgement: Quantifying stakeholder effects improves policy decisions, but must be combined with judgement about unquantifiable and distributional effects. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A legal maximum price set by the government below the equilibrium price to make a good more affordable"?
items.answer: price ceiling (maximum price)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of price ceiling (maximum price).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "welfare (deadweight) loss of a tax"?
options: The total amount spent by consumers on a good, equal to the price paid × quantity bought
An indirect tax of a fixed amount per unit of a good, which shifts the supply curve up parallel by the amount of the tax
Action by the government to change market outcomes, using taxes, subsidies, price controls, regulation, direct provision or nudges
The loss of social surplus caused by the reduction in quantity below the free-market equilibrium, not offset by tax revenue
items.answer: The loss of social surplus caused by the reduction in quantity below the free-market equilibrium, not offset by tax revenue
items.markingKey: D. "welfare (deadweight) loss of a tax" is the loss of social surplus caused by the reduction in quantity below the free-market equilibrium, not offset by tax revenue.

items.stem: Define the term "direct provision".
items.answer: The supply of goods and services by the government itself, such as state schools and public parks
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the supply of goods and services by the government itself, such as state schools and public parks. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between producer revenue (with a tax) and consumer expenditure.
items.answer: With a tax, consumer expenditure = price paid × quantity; producer revenue = price received × quantity. The difference is the tax revenue.
items.markingKey: With a tax, consumer expenditure = price paid × quantity; producer revenue = price received × quantity. The difference is the tax revenue. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Noah writes: "Price controls help all consumers because prices are lower." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Consumers who obtain the good at the lower price gain, but those who cannot buy it because of the shortage lose, and quality may fall; black markets may also develop.
items.markingKey: Consumers who obtain the good at the lower price gain, but those who cannot buy it because of the shortage lose, and quality may fall; black markets may also develop. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ana writes: "Subsidies only benefit producers because the money is paid to them." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The subsidy shifts supply down, lowering the price consumers pay, so consumers also gain; the split depends on elasticities.
items.markingKey: The subsidy shifts supply down, lowering the price consumers pay, so consumers also gain; the split depends on elasticities. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between command-and-control policies and market-based policies.
items.answer: Market-based policies (taxes, subsidies, tradable permits) change incentives through prices; command-and-control policies (regulation, bans, standards) directly require or forbid behaviour.
items.markingKey: Market-based policies (taxes, subsidies, tradable permits) change incentives through prices; command-and-control policies (regulation, bans, standards) directly require or forbid behaviour. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "The welfare loss of a tax equals the tax revenue." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Tax revenue is a transfer from consumers and producers to the government; the welfare loss is only the triangle of surplus lost on units no longer traded.
items.markingKey: Tax revenue is a transfer from consumers and producers to the government; the welfare loss is only the triangle of surplus lost on units no longer traded. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a price ceiling may lead to a parallel market.
items.answer: Consumers who cannot buy at the legal price are willing to pay more than the ceiling for the limited supply, so some sellers sell illegally at higher prices.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Consumers who cannot buy at the legal price are willing to pay more than the ceiling for the limited supply, so some sellers sell illegally at higher prices. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe US subsidies for corn ethanol and explain what it reveals about the effects of subsidies.
items.answer: Subsidies and mandates have led to around 40% of the US corn crop being used for ethanol. The subsidy increased supply and production, but diverted land from food crops, raised corn prices and imposed costs on taxpayers.
items.markingKey: Context (Subsidies and mandates have led to around 40% of the US corn crop being used for ethanol.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The subsidy increased supply and production, but diverted land from food crops, raised corn prices and imposed costs on taxpayers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effects of subsidies.

items.stem: Briefly describe Germany's €49 Deutschlandticket introduced in 2023 and explain what it reveals about subsidies as a form of government intervention.
items.answer: A subsidised monthly ticket allowing unlimited regional and local public transport, funded jointly by federal and state governments. The subsidy lowers the price of public transport to encourage use, reducing congestion and emissions, at a cost to taxpayers.
items.markingKey: Context (A subsidised monthly ticket allowing unlimited regional and local public transport, funded jointly by federal and state governments.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The subsidy lowers the price of public transport to encourage use, reducing congestion and emissions, at a cost to taxpayers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to subsidies as a form of government intervention.

items.stem: A researcher estimates that the weekly demand for cinema tickets in Mumbai is Qd = 180 − 4P and the weekly supply is Qs = −60 + 4P (P in $, Q in thousands). The government sets a minimum price of $35 and buys the surplus. Calculate the effect on (i) consumer expenditure, (ii) producer revenue and (iii) government spending, and identify which stakeholder gains most.
items.answer: (i) 1800 → 1400; (ii) 1800 → 2800; (iii) 1400; producers gain most
items.markingKey: Equilibrium P = 30, Q = 60 [1]; at $35: Qd = 40, Qs = 80 [1]; consumer expenditure 35×40 = 1400 [1]; producer revenue 35×80 = 2800 [1]; government spending 35×40 = 1400 [1]; producers gain (revenue +1000), consumers and taxpayers lose [1].

items.stem: With reference to Venezuela's price controls on basic foods, explain how it illustrates the consequences of price ceilings.
items.answer: Prices of flour, milk and other staples were fixed below market levels; by 2016 shelves were empty and long queues formed. Price below equilibrium cut quantity supplied and raised quantity demanded, creating shortages and black markets.
items.markingKey: Context (Prices of flour, milk and other staples were fixed below market levels; by 2016 shelves were empty and long queues formed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Price below equilibrium cut quantity supplied and raised quantity demanded, creating shortages and black markets. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the consequences of price ceilings.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the effects of a subsidy on producers of a good such as electric buses.
items.answer: Diagram: supply shifts down from S to S − subsidy; price to consumers falls from Pe to Pc, price received by producers rises to Pp = Pc + subsidy, quantity rises from Qe to Qs. Government spending = subsidy × Qs; gains to consumers and producers are shown, and a welfare loss triangle if there are no external benefits.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: supply shifts down from S to S − subsidy; price to consumers falls from Pe to Pc, price received by producers rises to Pp = Pc + subsidy, quantity rises from Qe to Qs. Government spending = subsidy × Qs; gains to consumers and producers are shown, and a welfare loss triangle if there are no external benefits. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: "Indirect taxes are only used to raise revenue." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Indirect taxes also aim to discourage consumption of harmful goods and correct negative externalities (e.g. carbon and sugar taxes).
items.markingKey: Indirect taxes also aim to discourage consumption of harmful goods and correct negative externalities (e.g. carbon and sugar taxes). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Minimum wages do more good than harm."
items.answer: Moderate minimum wages appear to raise incomes with little job loss, but very high minimum wages relative to median wages risk unemployment.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: raise incomes of low-paid workers and reduce in-work poverty; may increase productivity and reduce staff turnover; evidence (Card and Krueger; UK national living wage) suggests small employment effects. Arguments against: may cause unemployment for low-skilled and young workers; higher prices for consumers; may encourage informal employment in developing countries. Supported judgement: Moderate minimum wages appear to raise incomes with little job loss, but very high minimum wages relative to median wages risk unemployment.

items.stem: A researcher estimates that the weekly demand for rice in Singapore is Qd = 82 − 2P and the weekly supply is Qs = −30 + 2P (P in $, Q in thousands). To make it more affordable, the government is considering either (A) a maximum price of $27 or (B) a subsidy of $2 per unit to producers, which would lower the market price to the same $27. Calculate the quantity consumers would obtain under each policy and the cost of option B, and recommend one policy.
items.answer: A: quantity traded 24 (shortage 4); B: quantity 28, cost 56; B gives more output at a fiscal cost
items.markingKey: Equilibrium P = 28, Q = 26 [1]. A: at $27, Qs = 24, Qd = 28, shortage 4; only 24 units traded [2]. B: supply Qs = -30 + 2(P + 2); Pc = 27, Q = 28 [1]; cost 2 × 28 = 56 [1]. Recommendation weighs B's higher output and no shortage against its fiscal cost/opportunity cost; A costs nothing directly but causes shortages, queues and black markets [1].
